seedNote: Seeded ledger record for the Architecture v1.0 §13 continuity demonstration. Authored from real, live-retrieved Anthropic newsroom articles published on or before 2026-10-01. It was never published in a 012 edition and must not be presented as one.
thesis: Regulated institutions are moving coding agents from pilots to organisation-wide deployment, with legacy-system modernisation as the entry point; delivery partners that combine agent deployment with compliance and governance capacity are positioned to capture that work.
rationale: Two large regulated-sector commitments (a universal bank and a global IT-services firm) state organisation-wide adoption plans, but the figures are self-reported and the evidence base is one vendor's announcements.
targetActor: Technology-services firms and software vendors selling into banks, insurers and the public sector
decisionToConsider: Whether to build a governed legacy-modernisation offering around coding agents now, or wait for adoption evidence from more regulated buyers.
alternatives: The commitments reflect vendor-partner marketing rather than measured production adoption.
Regulated buyers will standardise on hyperscaler-bundled tools, leaving little room for independent delivery partners.
blocker: Adoption targets and usage figures are self-reported by the vendor and its customers; no independent measurement exists in the evidence.
falsificationTest: Track public statements from regulated institutions and government buyers until the review date; if none beyond the seed evidence announces organisation-wide coding-agent deployment with a measurable target, downgrade the position.
validationConditions: By the review date, at least one additional regulated-sector or public-sector organisation publicly commits to organisation-wide coding-agent use with a stated adoption target, user count or procurement vehicle.
Barclays or a comparable bank publicly reports reaching its stated Claude Code adoption target.
invalidationConditions: A regulator or a named regulated institution publicly restricts or rolls back coding-agent deployment for compliance or security reasons.
By the review date, no further regulated or public-sector organisation has made such a commitment public.
